lesson.title: Giving a Stateless Protocol a Memory
lesson.summary: Cookies let a server recognize the same client across multiple requests by sending a small piece of data with a Set-Cookie header that the browser stores and automatically resends, patching over the fact that HTTP itself has no memory.
lesson.body:
The protocol chapter pointed out that HTTP is stateless: by itself, a server handling one request has no idea whether it is talking to a brand new client or one it has already exchanged ten requests with. That is a real problem for anything that needs to remember a client between requests, staying logged in being the obvious example, and cookies are the mechanism HTTP applications use to solve it.

The mechanism rides entirely on the headers described in the previous chapter. A server that wants to remember a client sends a Set-Cookie response header containing a name and value, something like session_id=abc123. The browser stores that pair. On every later request to a matching site, the browser automatically attaches a Cookie request header carrying that same name and value back to the server, and the server can look up whatever it stored under that ID, no memory required inside HTTP itself, all of the state lives in the cookie and in the server's own records.

A Set-Cookie header usually carries more than just the name and value, in the form of attributes that control how the cookie behaves. Expires or Max-Age set how long the cookie should be kept, with Max-Age given as a number of seconds and generally taking precedence when both are present. Domain and Path scope exactly which requests the cookie gets attached to. Secure means the browser will only ever send the cookie over HTTPS. HttpOnly means client side JavaScript cannot read the cookie's value at all, which limits what an attacker can steal even if they manage to inject a script into the page. SameSite restricts whether the cookie gets sent along with requests originating from other sites, which helps limit a category of attack that tricks a logged in browser into making unwanted requests.

A login flow shows the whole cycle. A client sends POST /login with a correct username and password, and the server responds 200 OK along with:
Set-Cookie: session_id=abc123; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Max-Age=3600

From that point on, for the next hour, every request the browser sends to that site automatically includes:
Cookie: session_id=abc123

and the server looks abc123 up in its own session store to know exactly who is making the request, without the client having to log in again on every page load.

Cookies are not the only way to carry state on top of HTTP, plenty of systems pass a token in an Authorization header instead, but cookies were the original solution and remain the most common way an ordinary web browser stays recognized across an entire session.
